443.bp: Web systems often depend on sensor and device streams that are supposed to arrive as orderly measurements over time: temperatures, traffic counts, device signals, user activity traces, or other repeated readings. In practice, those streams have holes. A packet is delayed, a device fails, a logger skips a value, or a network boundary drops part of the record. The missing numbers are not cosmetic. An anomaly detector may miss the beginning of a failure, a recommendation system may read stale behavior as current, and an A/B test may compare groups using broken measurements. FSDI serves the repair step before those later decisions. Its question is: when part of a time series is missing, how can a system fill the gap in a way that respects the rhythm of the original stream? The paper focuses on diffusion, meaning a learned process that practices adding noise to data and then learns to remove that noise to reconstruct plausible values.
443.wh: The hard part is that a time series is not just a row of independent numbers. It has slow movement, repeated cycles, sharp changes, and small fast wiggles mixed together. One stream may carry most of its useful energy in daily cycles; another may have irregular peaks spread across several time scales. Existing frequency-aware diffusion methods, according to the abstract, mostly change the input or the network shape while leaving the forward noise schedule unchanged. That means the corruption step injects the same amount of noise into every frequency bin, where a bin is one bucket of rhythm after the signal is rewritten as slow and fast components. Equal treatment sounds fair, but it ignores the data's actual shape. Real spectral energy does not follow a clean low-versus-high split. If the repair process corrupts every rhythm the same way, it can underprotect important rhythms and overemphasize weak ones.
443.naive: A smart beginner might first fill each missing point by drawing a smooth line between the observed points, or by copying nearby values from the same time of day. That can work when the stream changes gently and the gap is short. It fails when the missing segment contains a peak, a periodic swing, or a mixture of slow and fast behavior. A second beginner move would be to use a standard diffusion imputer and let the model learn everything from examples. FSDI argues that this also leaves a mismatch: the model may be frequency-aware in its inputs, but its noising process still damages each frequency bucket equally, even though the original stream does not store equal energy in each bucket.
443.ap: FSDI's central move is to shape the noise before the model learns to remove it. Instead of applying one uniform variance schedule to all parts of the signal, it first looks at the training data in the frequency domain. In plain terms, it rewrites each time series as a mixture of rhythms and measures how much energy each rhythm usually carries. Then it assigns noise variances by taking the inverse of that energy: rhythms that already carry strong signal get less relative corruption, while weaker rhythms can receive more. The schedule is not allowed to change the total difficulty of the diffusion task. The paper uses Parseval calibration, meaning it adjusts the frequency-side noise so the total noise energy matches standard diffusion. The result is still comparable to the usual method, but the noise is distributed according to the data's actual spectral shape.
443.mech: The mechanism starts with incomplete time-series data from web, sensor, or IoT settings. During training, the observed series are examined through their spectrum, which is a way of describing a signal by rhythms rather than by raw time positions. Each frequency bin represents one range of oscillation speed, from slow trends to faster variation. FSDI estimates how much spectral energy the data places in each bin. That estimate becomes a map of which rhythms are naturally strong and which are weak. Next, the method builds a frequency-shaped variance schedule. Variance here means the amount of random disturbance added during the forward diffusion process. Instead of adding the same disturbance everywhere, FSDI allocates bin-level noise as the inverse of the measured energy. It then calibrates the schedule with Parseval's identity, the rule that total energy is preserved when a signal is moved between the time view and the frequency view, so the full amount of noise remains equal to standard diffusion. After this, the model learns the reverse process: given a partly observed series and a deliberately corrupted version, remove noise step by step and produce filled-in values for the missing positions. The output is an imputed time series intended to support later anomaly detection, recommendation, or A/B testing.
443.math: The first mathematical object is a time series, an ordered list where position matters because nearby and repeated readings carry meaning. The second is the frequency view of that same list. A frequency transform asks: if this stream were made by combining waves of different speeds, how much of each speed would be present? Spectral energy is the strength assigned to those rhythms. FSDI uses that energy as evidence for how the corruption process should behave. Diffusion contributes a second idea: learn repair by first learning controlled damage. A forward process adds noise according to a schedule, and a reverse process learns how to undo that damage. The paper changes the schedule, not merely the model input. Variance is the size of the random shake applied at a step. By giving each frequency bin its own variance, FSDI turns a single global corruption rule into a data-shaped one. The inverse-energy allocation is a balancing rule: if a rhythm is already strong, do not bury it under equal noise; if it is weak, the model can tolerate more disturbance there. Parseval calibration supplies the accounting constraint: the total noise energy stays the same across representations. The tradeoff is preserving meaningful rhythm versus keeping the training task stable and fairly comparable.
443.dots: FSDI sits at the crossing of two recurring conference ideas. In the time-series and spatiotemporal family, it shares the belief that order and rhythm must be protected before a system can forecast, detect, or repair. Nearby local summaries mention KFTD, GFMixer, Fourier-Galerkin modeling, and point-to-point spectral forecasting as sibling efforts that also treat repeated patterns as structure, not decoration. In the generative and diffusion family, it belongs with papers that fill missing objects under constraints rather than simply choosing an existing answer. TRACE is a nearby repair example for movement values, while FSDI repairs sensor-like streams by preserving frequency energy. It also connects to anomaly detection and recommendation because the abstract names those downstream tasks: a repaired stream becomes evidence for later warnings, rankings, or experiments. The shared deeper problem is controlled completion: create the missing part without violating the structure that made the original record useful.
443.ww: The method should help because the corruption process becomes aligned with the thing being repaired. A standard diffusion imputer asks the model to learn from damage that is spread uniformly across frequency bins. If the real data concentrates signal unevenly, that training task teaches the model under an artificial kind of damage. FSDI instead makes the noising step respect the empirical energy map of the data. The reverse model then practices removing noise from rhythms in proportions that better match the streams it will repair. The Parseval calibration matters because it prevents an easy but misleading win: reducing total noise would make the task simpler but not comparable. By keeping total noise energy equal, FSDI changes where the noise goes, not how much total damage exists. This gives the model more informative practice on the spectral shape of the data while preserving the training stability the abstract says standard diffusion already has. In everyday terms, it repairs a song by respecting which notes carry the tune and which are faint background detail.
443.po: The payoff is a more faithful imputation step for real web analytics pipelines where missing time-series values can damage later decisions. The abstract reports experiments on real-world datasets and says FSDI achieves state-of-the-art performance. Grounded in the paper's stated task, that means the filled values better preserve the measured stream than generic diffusion variants that use a uniform variance schedule. The practical gain is not just a lower error number: cleaner repaired streams give anomaly detection, recommendation, and A/B testing less distorted evidence to work from.
443.limits: The claim depends on the training data's spectral energy being a useful guide for future missing segments. If the stream changes its rhythms after a device replacement, policy change, event shock, or new logging rule, the learned frequency schedule may point to the wrong structure. The abstract does not specify the datasets, missingness patterns, or which downstream tasks were directly tested. It also reports public code and strong experimental performance but does not prove that inverse-energy allocation is best for every sensor domain, every gap length, or nonstationary streams whose frequency content keeps moving.

444.bp: Many web systems must describe the same object from several sources at once. A video can have images, text, audio, user comments, and behavior logs; a product can have photos, seller text, category clues, and click history. The task is not just to choose one label, because one object may belong to many labels at the same time. The paper studies this multi-source, many-label setting under two pressures that ordinary deployments create. First, some sources are often missing: a page may have text but no image, or an item may have behavior logs but no clean description. Second, new labels keep appearing as the web changes. A model that only understands the old label set becomes stale. E2PL is meant for this combined situation: keep learning new classes while still making predictions when arbitrary views are absent, without letting the number of learned settings explode.
444.wh: The hard part is that missing sources and new labels multiply each other's difficulty. If every item always arrived with the same views, the model could learn a stable recipe for combining them. If the label set never changed, it could tune itself around one fixed vocabulary of possible answers. Real web data violates both comforts. Different examples can lose different views, so the system must know how to act when image is missing, when text is missing, when both are present, or when several other combinations occur. At the same time, class-incremental learning asks the model to add new labels without discarding its old competence. A direct missing-view design can create separate settings for every subset of views, but the number of subsets doubles whenever another view is added. That is the exponential parameter growth the abstract names, and it makes web-scale use impractical.
444.naive: A smart beginner might train one classifier for the complete data and then patch missing cases with simple fixes: fill absent views with zeros, ignore the missing source, or train a separate small model for each pattern of available views. The first two fixes blur together very different situations. A zero image is not the same as no image, and ignoring a source can hide which evidence is trustworthy. The separate-model idea respects the missing pattern, but it breaks as soon as there are many views, because every combination needs its own learned parameters. The beginner might also retrain whenever new classes appear, but that is expensive and can overwrite what the system already learned about old labels.
444.ap: E2PL's central move is to guide a shared model with small learned instructions rather than build a new full model for every situation. A prompt here means a compact learned piece of input-side guidance that tells the model what kind of task or missing-view condition it is facing. The paper uses task-tailored prompts for the arrival of new classes and missing-aware prompts for whichever views are absent. The important efficiency move is prototype tensorization. Instead of storing a separate missing-aware prompt for every possible subset of views, E2PL represents those prompts from smaller atomic parts and combines the parts. Atomic tensor decomposition is the mathematical language for this: it describes a large table of combinations through a limited set of reusable factors, reducing parameter growth from exponential in the number of views to linear.
444.mech: The input is a multi-view, multi-label example: several possible sources describe one web object, some of those sources may be unavailable, and the correct answer may include several labels. The learning setting also unfolds over time, because new classes are introduced after earlier classes have already been learned. E2PL first separates the guidance problem into two kinds of prompts. Task-tailored prompts tell the model how to adapt to the current class-incremental task, so the system can attach new label knowledge without treating the whole problem as frozen. Missing-aware prompts tell the model what evidence pattern it is seeing, so an item with only text is not handled the same way as an item with text plus image. The expensive version would prepare a distinct prompt for every missing-view pattern. E2PL instead builds those prompts through prototype tensorization: each view contributes compact atomic pieces, and a prompt for a particular missing pattern is assembled from the relevant pieces. The dynamic contrastive learning strategy then compares different missing-view patterns so the model learns their dependencies, meaning it is pushed to keep related cases close in behavior while still respecting their differences. The output is a multi-label prediction over the current class set, with fewer learned prompt parameters than the exhaustive missing-pattern design would require.
444.math: The main mathematical idea is factorization: describe a large set of possible combinations using smaller reusable parts. If there are many views, the list of present-or-missing patterns grows like a branching tree; each added view doubles the number of possible patterns. A full table with one prompt per pattern wastes memory because many patterns share structure. Atomic tensor decomposition treats that table as something built from atoms. In everyday terms, it is like describing many outfits by shirts, pants, and shoes instead of listing every complete outfit separately. The paper uses this to turn missing-view prompt parameters from exponential growth into linear growth with respect to the number of views. A second idea is comparison-based learning, called contrastive learning in the abstract: the model is trained by comparing cases or patterns so that related forms of evidence agree more than unrelated ones. Here the comparison is dynamic because missing patterns differ across examples and tasks. The underlying tradeoff is compression versus detail. Tensorization saves parameters by sharing parts, but the shared parts must still preserve the meaningful differences between missing-view situations. The class-incremental side adds the stability-versus-adaptation tradeoff: learn new labels while keeping old label behavior useful.
444.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of several recurring conference problems. It is about multi-view learning because the object is described by several sources whose evidence must be combined. It is about multi-label classification because the answer is a set of labels rather than a single winner. It is about incremental learning because the label universe expands over time, a pressure also visible in repo entries on graph incremental learning and continual named entity recognition, where new classes arrive without permission to forget old ones. It is also an efficiency paper, because the key obstacle is not only prediction quality but the cost of representing every missing-view pattern separately. The connection to similarity and comparison appears in the dynamic contrastive part: different incomplete versions of the same broader situation must teach the model what should remain consistent. The connection to compression appears in tensor decomposition, which keeps the reusable structure and avoids storing every combination by hand.
444.ww: The approach should improve over the naive design because it matches the shape of the problem. Missing views are not random labels that require unrelated models; they are combinations of the same underlying sources. If a system has learned how the text view behaves and how the image view behaves, it should reuse that knowledge when only one is missing or when both are present. Prototype tensorization gives the model a way to reuse those view-level parts instead of memorizing every subset separately. Task-tailored prompts help with the other pressure: new classes can be introduced through compact task guidance rather than rebuilding the whole classifier from scratch each time. The dynamic comparison step helps because missing patterns are related but not identical. It asks the model to notice that two incomplete versions may still refer to the same object-level meaning, while also learning when a missing source removes important evidence. This is why the method can plausibly be both effective and efficient: it shares structure where the world really shares structure.
444.po: The payoff is a model for the paper's newly formalized task, incomplete multi-view multi-label class incremental learning. According to the abstract, E2PL handles heterogeneous missing views and expanding classes together, while avoiding the parameter explosion that makes exhaustive missing-pattern prompts hard to scale. The concrete efficiency claim is that prototype tensorization reduces prompt parameter complexity from exponential to linear with respect to the number of views. The abstract also reports experiments on three benchmarks where E2PL outperforms prior methods in both effectiveness and efficiency. For web applications, that means a practical route to updating label vocabularies while still using messy, partially observed multi-source data.
444.limits: The claims depend on the missing-view structure being shareable through atomic parts. If some missing patterns require entirely different reasoning, the compressed tensor representation may hide too much detail. The approach also assumes prompts can carry enough task and missingness information without full retraining. The abstract does not specify the three benchmarks, the kinds of views, the degree of missingness, or how new classes are scheduled, so the deployment boundary is unclear from this evidence alone. It reports better effectiveness and efficiency, but the abstract does not prove behavior under adversarial missingness, highly rare labels, noisy views, or settings where old and new classes conflict strongly.

445.bp: A large food, delivery, or local-services app has to choose what each person should see next from an enormous catalog of restaurants, dishes, shops, coupons, and services. In a newer generative recommender, the system does not only score every item one by one. It can generate a compact item code, called a semantic ID, that stands for the kind of thing being recommended. The hope is that this code carries meaning from a large language model, such as food type or service intent, while making the output space smaller and easier to generate. This paper serves that practical problem at Meituan scale: make those generated item codes faithful enough that they help recommendations for hundreds of millions of mobile users, rather than becoming a convenient but lossy shorthand.
445.wh: The hard part is that a semantic ID has to live in two worlds at once. First, it has to summarize item meaning in a small codebook, which is a dictionary of allowed codes. Second, it has to be useful inside the generation process that decides what to recommend for a particular user and situation. Existing methods, according to the abstract, leave a gap between the codebook space and the generation space because the code is not aware enough of the context in which it will be generated. A code that looks meaningful by itself may not be the code the generator can use well for this user. The second difficulty is compression. Quantization, meaning replacing rich numeric descriptions with a limited set of code choices, can erase detail from language-model meaning. If the lost detail is exactly what distinguishes two restaurants or services, recommendation quality drops.
445.naive: A smart beginner might ask a language model to describe each item, turn that description into a compact code, and train the recommender to generate those codes. This seems reasonable because the code is smaller than the full catalog and may carry human-like meaning. It fails when the code is built mostly from item semantics alone. Recommendation is not only about what an item is; it is about which users choose which items in which contexts. If the codebook ignores those collaborative signals, meaning signals learned from many user-item interactions, the generator learns in one coordinate system while the codes were made in another. Naive rounding into codes also throws away subtle semantic differences.
445.ap: DOS makes two connected moves. First, it uses a user-item dual-flow design, meaning it lets signals from users and items shape the semantic IDs together instead of treating item meaning as isolated text knowledge. The abstract says this collaborative signal aligns the semantic ID codebook space with the generation space. In plain terms, the dictionary of item codes is trained to fit the same recommendation situation in which the generator will later use it. Second, DOS changes the compression step. Its orthogonal residual quantization rotates the semantic space before assigning codes. A rotation preserves distances and information in principle, like turning a map on the table without tearing it, but it can place the important directions in a better orientation for coding. Residual coding then stores what earlier code choices failed to capture.
445.mech: The mechanism starts with item and user evidence available in a production recommender: item-side semantic information influenced by large language models, user-item interaction patterns from Meituan, and the generation task that must output useful semantic IDs. First, DOS builds or uses a semantic space, a numeric arrangement where items with related meaning should be near one another. Second, instead of creating item codes in isolation, it runs a dual flow over users and items. The user side brings collaborative evidence: many people choosing, skipping, or interacting with items create a practical signal about which items behave similarly in recommendations. The item side carries semantic evidence from language-model knowledge. Third, these flows are used to align the codebook with the generation space, so the codes the generator learns to produce are not detached from the codes that preserve item meaning. Fourth, DOS compresses the semantic descriptions through orthogonal residual quantization. It rotates the numeric space to an orientation where quantization loses less important meaning. Then it assigns a code for a coarse part of the description and uses residual steps to encode remaining error left after earlier choices. The output is a semantic ID for recommendation that is both compact enough for generation and better matched to user-item behavior.
445.math: The first mathematical idea is similarity: each item and possibly each user context is represented by numbers so the system can compare what should be treated as close. Here, closeness must mean more than shared words in an item description; it must also reflect patterns of people choosing items. The second idea is quantization, which is compression by choosing from a limited dictionary. It turns many possible numeric descriptions into a smaller set of codes, saving generation effort but risking semantic loss. The third idea is residual coding. Instead of forcing one code to explain everything, the system can encode a first approximation and then encode the leftover error, so fine detail is not abandoned immediately. The fourth idea is orthogonal rotation. Orthogonal means the transformation changes orientation while preserving lengths and angles, so it can reorganize coordinates without destroying the underlying relationships. The paper uses this because a codebook can be bad simply because the important variation is pointed awkwardly relative to the coding grid. The tradeoff is compression versus detail, plus semantic meaning versus collaborative usefulness. DOS tries to keep the code small while preserving the distinctions that matter for ranking recommendations.
445.dots: This paper belongs to the recommender-system family in the repo because it is another answer to the shared pressure of choosing a small useful set from a huge, changing pile. It also connects to the generative-recommendation branch described in the generative family: generation is being used as controlled completion, where the missing object is the next useful item code rather than an image or molecule. The closest concepts are similarity and ranking. Similarity appears because semantic IDs make a map where related items and user needs should land near one another. Ranking appears because the generated codes ultimately affect which items rise into the few recommendations a user sees. It also touches efficiency and information compression: the system uses a compact codebook to reduce generation difficulty, but must avoid compressing away the signals that distinguish Meituan items in real use.
445.ww: DOS should improve over the naive approach because it repairs the mismatch between how codes are made and how they are used. If item codes are made only from language-model meaning, they can be clean descriptions but poor recommendation handles. A dessert shop and a dinner restaurant may be semantically related as food businesses, yet user behavior may separate them sharply by time, need, price, or occasion. The dual-flow design gives the codebook a way to absorb those collaborative differences while still keeping semantic meaning. The orthogonal residual quantization helps for a different reason. Compression error is not evenly harmful. Losing a detail that users do not care about may be acceptable; losing the detail that separates substitute items from unrelated items is damaging. By rotating the space, DOS tries to place important variation where the code choices can preserve it. By encoding residual error, it avoids treating the first coarse code as the whole story. The result is a compact ID that should be easier to generate without becoming too blunt for recommendation.
445.po: The payoff is a more usable semantic-ID layer for generative recommendation in a real industrial system. The abstract reports extensive offline experiments and online A/B testing, so the claim is not limited to a toy setup or a single offline ranking table. It also says the method has been deployed in Meituan's mobile application and serves hundreds of millions of users. Grounded only in the abstract, the practical capability is clear: DOS makes generated semantic IDs better aligned with user-item recommendation behavior while preserving more semantic information during compression.
445.limits: The abstract does not give the exact datasets, metrics, A/B-test duration, effect sizes, or failure cases, so the strength of the reported improvement cannot be judged from this input alone. DOS assumes collaborative signals are reliable guides to recommendation meaning; if user behavior is biased by previous exposure, promotions, geography, or platform policy, the codebook may preserve those biases. It also assumes the semantic space from large language models contains useful item knowledge worth compressing. Orthogonal residual quantization can reduce loss only if the important semantic directions can be made easier to code by rotation and residual steps. The abstract does not prove transfer beyond Meituan's setting.

446.bp: A recommender is trying to answer a question whose answer is not written anywhere: given this person's past interactions, what are they likely to want next? Ordinary retrieval-augmented generation is built for a different kind of task. If someone asks for a fact, the system can search a document collection, bring back passages that contain the answer, and ask a language model to write from those passages. Preference prediction is stranger. The useful evidence is not a sentence saying the user will like the target item. It is the pattern between what the user touched before and what is being considered now. This paper serves that gap. PRAG keeps the retrieval idea, but turns retrieved history into personalized evidence for an unknown outcome. In the recommendation setting described in the abstract, it asks the language model to reason from user-specific similarity signals instead of treating prediction like factual lookup.
446.wh: The hard part is that a user's preference is both personal and indirect. A past click, purchase, rating, or interaction does not simply state a future choice; it gives a clue about taste under some earlier circumstance. Standard RAG is useful when the answer can be directly retrieved, but here the answer must be inferred from how well past behavior matches the target information. The system also has to avoid two opposite mistakes. If it ignores the user's history, the language model falls back toward general item knowledge and may recommend something broadly plausible but personally wrong. If it dumps all history into the prompt as equally important, old or weakly related interactions can drown out the few past choices that actually explain the current candidate. The central tension is therefore not just retrieval quality. It is deciding which pieces of a person's history should carry more force when the model predicts an outcome that has not happened yet.
446.naive: A smart beginner would build a factual RAG pipeline for recommendation: collect the user's history, retrieve related item descriptions or past interactions, paste them into the prompt, and ask the language model whether the target fits. That is sensible because outside evidence often helps language models avoid made-up or stale answers. It fails because recommendation evidence is not all equal. One past item may reveal the same preference behind the target, while another may share only a surface word or a broad category. A plain prompt gives the model text, but not a clear signal about which historical interactions deserve more trust. The model may then average together unrelated history, overreact to verbose items, or produce a generic preference judgment.
446.ap: The paper's core move is to make similarity between history and target an explicit control signal for the prompt. PRAG computes how semantically similar a user's historical interactions are to the target information. Semantic similarity means a measured judgment of whether two pieces of information mean related things for the task, not just whether they share exact words. PRAG then adaptively integrates that similarity as prompt weights. In plain terms, the prompt does not present every historical clue with the same volume. Interactions that look more relevant to the current target can speak more loudly, while weaker matches can recede. This turns RAG from answer retrieval into evidence weighting for prediction. The language model still generates or judges using its general language ability, but the user-specific preference signal is placed directly in front of it in a structured way.
446.mech: The mechanism starts with two kinds of input: a user's historical interactions and the target information for the candidate whose outcome should be predicted. The history is the evidence about the person. The target is the thing being judged now. PRAG first compares the target against the historical interactions by semantic similarity, asking which previous interactions are meaningfully close to the current candidate. The abstract does not specify the exact scoring formula, so the grounded claim is that the system computes similarity scores rather than treating history as an unordered pile. Next, those scores are converted into prompt weights. A weight is a controlled amount of influence: high similarity means the corresponding historical clue should matter more in the prompt, while lower similarity means it should matter less. The weighted prompt is then given to a large language model inside an LLM-based application. In the recommender-system version, the model receives not only item and history text, but also a shaped signal about personal relevance. The output is a prediction of user preference or recommendation performance, not a retrieved factual answer. The paper evaluates this process with two language-model backbones and four real-world datasets, comparing whether this weighted predictive setup improves recommendation.
446.math: The main mathematical idea is measured closeness under uncertainty. Each historical interaction and each target item must be described in a form that allows comparison by meaning. That description is often called an embedding, meaning a compact list of numbers that places an object in a comparison map; what matters here is not the word, but the act of making two pieces of information close when they carry similar preference meaning. Similarity then turns a messy question, which past behavior is relevant now, into a score for each historical clue. Weighting is the second idea. A weight is a multiplier of influence, like letting some witnesses speak louder because their testimony concerns the same kind of case. The third idea is prediction: the system estimates an unknown future or hidden outcome from partial evidence rather than retrieving a stored answer. These ideas fit recommendation because preference is usually inferred from repeated behavior. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. A similarity score helps the model focus, but it also squeezes rich histories into numbers, so the system must trust that the chosen notion of closeness preserves the preference signal that matters.
446.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of three recurring conference ideas. From the RAG family, it keeps the principle that a language model should not answer from internal memory alone; outside evidence should shape the response. But it changes what evidence means: instead of retrieving facts, it retrieves and weighs personal history for an unknown outcome. From the recommender-systems family, it shares the larger pressure of choosing useful items from a huge pile when clicks, interactions, and item descriptions only partially reveal taste. From the similarity and ranking concepts, it uses closeness to decide which past interactions should influence the current prediction, and it supports the downstream act of sorting or selecting candidates. It also touches probability and learning from examples, because the system is estimating a likely preference from repeated cases. Its neighboring papers may handle hallucination, evidence quality, or retrieval cost, while PRAG handles a different failure: factual retrieval machinery being used for a predictive task.
446.ww: PRAG can work because it gives the language model the missing structure that a plain prompt lacks. A user's history is useful only when the model can tell which parts of it transfer to the current target. Similarity scores provide that bridge. If a candidate is close in meaning to several past interactions, those interactions become stronger evidence that the user's earlier taste applies here. If the candidate is far from much of the history, the model is less encouraged to force a connection. This is better than the naive approach because the model is not left to infer all relevance from raw text order and wording. It receives a shaped signal about personal importance before producing the prediction. The method also fits the abstract's claim that predictive RAG differs from factual RAG: there is no answer passage to copy, so the system must improve the evidence pattern that supports inference. Weighting history by target similarity makes that inference more explicit and less generic.
446.po: The payoff is a RAG-style method that can be used beyond factual question answering. In the paper's recommender-system instantiation, PRAG explicitly captures user-specific preference signals through semantic similarity modelling and feeds them into the prompt as adaptive weights. The abstract reports experiments with two LLM backbones and four real-world datasets, where PRAG significantly improves predictive recommendation performance. The practical capability is not just a better generated explanation. It is a way for LLM-based applications to make personalized predictions when the desired answer is not stored in a document but must be inferred from a person's prior interactions.
446.limits: The method assumes that the user's historical interactions contain real preference evidence and that semantic similarity can identify which parts of that history matter for the target. It can fail when past interactions are sparse, noisy, stale, or caused by exposure rather than genuine preference. It also assumes prompt weights are interpreted by the language model in the intended way; the abstract does not prove how stable that behavior is across all models or domains. The reported evidence covers two LLM backbones and four real-world datasets, but the abstract does not specify long-term user welfare, cold-start behavior, fairness effects, privacy risk from using histories, or whether the similarity scores remain reliable when item meanings or user tastes change.

447.bp: Many data-hungry systems now face an awkward bargain. Real text written by people is costly to gather, can expose private facts, and may be locked inside product or research pipelines. Synthetic text offers a tempting substitute: ask a generative model to produce reviews, comments, or paper-review-like examples, then train another model on that cheaper collection. The danger is that the generator tends to repeat the common middle of the source collection. Unusual styles, difficult cases, rare opinions, and high-uncertainty examples can fade out. This paper studies that failure as model collapse: repeated reuse of generated outputs contracts the learned distribution, meaning the generated collection covers a narrower slice of the original world. DASGen is built for the practical job of making synthetic text that still covers rare tail regions, not just fluent common cases, so downstream training data remains broad enough for long-tailed applications.
447.wh: The hard part is that rare text is rare for a reason: there are few examples, and a generator has learned that common patterns are safer. If a Yelp-like review collection mostly contains ordinary restaurant comments, a model can generate many plausible ordinary reviews while barely touching unusual phrasing, edge-case sentiment, uncommon topics, or difficult reviewer behavior. That looks acceptable if one only checks fluency or average quality. It fails when the synthetic data becomes training material, because the next model sees a world with the uncommon parts weakened or missing. The abstract gives a concrete sign: when models are iteratively trained on their own synthetic outputs, the upper tail of the perplexity distribution compresses, with high-percentile values dropping by nearly half. Perplexity here is a measure of how unsurprising text looks to a model. If the most surprising examples become much less surprising, diversity has been squeezed out.
447.naive: A smart beginner would generate a large synthetic corpus with a strong hosted language model, perhaps using broad prompts such as "write more Yelp reviews" or "write more ICLR reviews," then mix those outputs into training. If the generated text is grammatical and resembles the domain, the beginner might assume more data means better coverage. The failure is that volume does not guarantee variety. A generator can produce thousands of examples while circling the same common region of the data. Another beginner fix is random prompting, but randomness still follows the model's learned habit of choosing likely continuations. Without a deliberate way to find and refill underrepresented regions, synthetic data can make the training set cleaner-looking while quietly erasing rare features.
447.ap: DASGen's central move is to treat synthetic generation as a coverage problem before treating it as a writing problem. First it looks for parts of the existing data distribution that are underrepresented. The abstract says it does this through embedding-space mining: it turns texts into learned numeric descriptions of meaning and style, then searches that map for regions that need more examples. That term matters only after translation: the method is building a map where nearby texts are treated as similar, then asking which neighborhoods are thin. Second, it steers a frozen, hosted language model with semantically structured prompts, so the generator is directed toward those thin neighborhoods. Third, it uses a discriminative diversity objective, a scoring rule that rewards outputs that add distinguishable variety rather than merely sounding normal. The base model is not retrained; the intervention is in selection, prompting, and diversity-guided generation.
447.mech: The input is an existing text collection from a domain such as Yelp reviews or ICLR'25 reviews, plus access to a hosted large language model that can generate new text. DASGen first represents each real example as a point in a comparison map, where distance is meant to capture semantic similarity. Because the abstract calls the method tail-aware, the next step is to search this map for tail regions: neighborhoods that exist in the source distribution but have weak coverage or are at risk of being lost when ordinary generation overproduces common cases. Those regions become generation targets. Instead of asking the language model for generic new reviews, DASGen builds semantically structured prompts that describe the kind of content needed from a target region. The language model remains frozen, meaning its internal weights are not updated; DASGen controls it from the outside. Candidate generated texts are then judged by a discriminative diversity objective. In plain terms, the system compares candidates against the desired rare region and against one another, preferring examples that enrich the tail rather than duplicate already common text. The output is a synthetic corpus intended to be distribution-aligned: it should resemble the source collection while deliberately restoring coverage of rare regions. The evaluations then check tail coverage and downstream accuracy on Yelp and ICLR'25 review settings.
447.math: The first mathematical idea is distribution matching. A distribution is the shape of a collection: which kinds of examples are common, which are rare, and how far the rare cases stretch from the center. DASGen is not only asking whether each generated text is plausible; it is asking whether the whole generated pile has a similar shape to the original pile, especially in the tail. The second idea is similarity geometry. Texts are compressed into numeric descriptions so the system can measure which examples are near one another. This compression is useful because it turns vague semantic coverage into a searchable map, but it can lose details if the map preserves the wrong kind of likeness. The third idea is tail measurement. The abstract uses the upper tail of the perplexity distribution as evidence of diversity loss: highly surprising texts should remain present if the collection still contains difficult or unusual cases. The fourth idea is objective-guided selection. A discriminative diversity objective defines what counts as better synthetic text, not as a human aesthetic judgment but as a score that favors distinct, tail-enriching candidates. The central tradeoff is coverage versus fidelity: generated examples must move into rare regions without drifting into text that no longer belongs to the domain.
447.dots: This paper connects to the conference's language-model and text-mining work because it asks whether generated language preserves the evidence structure of the collection it came from. It sits near similarity papers because its first step depends on a map of texts where distance stands in for semantic relatedness, and the success of tail mining depends on that map being faithful. It also connects to probability and information ideas: the tail is about unlikely or surprising cases, and the paper treats the disappearance of high-perplexity examples as an information loss, not just a cosmetic change in writing style. Compared with retrieval and recommendation papers that choose useful items from a large pile, DASGen chooses useful generation targets from a source distribution. Compared with privacy-motivated synthetic-data work, it accepts the privacy and curation appeal of synthetic content but argues that usefulness depends on preserving rare features that generic generation tends to smooth away.
447.ww: The approach should work better than naive generation because it interrupts the self-reinforcing preference for common cases. A general language model is good at producing fluent examples that fit the center of a domain, because those are the patterns it can satisfy with high confidence. DASGen first asks where the center is not enough. By mining the semantic map, it turns an invisible absence into explicit targets: these are the regions where more examples are needed. Structured prompts then give the frozen model a narrower assignment than open-ended generation, so it is more likely to produce text with the intended rare properties. The diversity objective adds a second guardrail. If two generated candidates say the same kind of thing in slightly different wording, they do not add much coverage; if a candidate occupies a thin but relevant region, it is more valuable. This matches the mechanism to the failure mode. Model collapse is a shrinking of variety, so DASGen spends its effort widening the generated collection where shrinkage is most damaging.
447.po: The payoff is a training-free way to make synthetic text corpora that better preserve long-tail coverage. The abstract reports strong tail coverage on two review settings: 98.54% on Yelp and 92.00% on ICLR'25, along with improved downstream accuracy compared with competitive baselines. The practical capability is not merely producing more text. It is producing synthetic data that remains useful when rare features matter, while still fitting into existing data pipelines because the hosted language model is frozen and no retraining of that generator is required. For teams using synthetic data to reduce curation cost or privacy exposure, DASGen gives a concrete method for checking and repairing a major failure mode.
447.limits: The claims depend on the text map capturing the rare features that matter. If the learned numeric descriptions group examples by surface wording while missing the real tail property, DASGen may enrich the wrong regions. The method also assumes that semantically structured prompts can make a frozen hosted model produce valid rare-region examples rather than strained or unrealistic text. The abstract reports Yelp and ICLR'25 review evaluations, so broader domains are not proven here. It gives tail coverage and downstream accuracy, but does not establish privacy guarantees, human quality judgments, behavior under adversarial prompts, or whether generated tail examples preserve every factual and cultural detail present in real rare cases.

448.bp: An edge IoT workflow is a chain of small services running near the physical world: a sensor provides data, an inference engine interprets it, and a message broker moves the result onward. The practical problem is not only whether those services exist, but whether a workflow can still find and bind to them while the network is breaking into islands, devices are coming and going, and every provider describes its capability in a slightly different vocabulary. SemaReg serves that moment. It treats service discovery as a resilience problem: when the exact requested service cannot be reached, the system should know whether another available service is close enough in meaning to satisfy the same step. The paper builds a registry for edge environments where knowledge about services is copied across replicas and interpreted through semantic type relationships, so orchestration can continue even when the infrastructure is only partly connected.
448.wh: The hard part is that service lookup at the edge is both a naming problem and a communication problem. A normal registry assumes the requester can ask a known place for a known type. Edge networks violate both assumptions. A partition can hide the registry or the preferred service. Service churn means an answer that was true a moment ago may now be stale. Heterogeneous capability descriptions mean two services may do compatible work without using the same exact label. If a workflow asks for one type and the registry only accepts exact type equality, the lookup fails even when a subtype could perform the same functional requirement. If the system only broadcasts requests, it spends communication widely and still may not reach the right island of the network. SemaReg has to keep useful service knowledge available locally, tolerate stale observations, and decide when a semantically compatible substitute is acceptable.
448.naive: A smart beginner would build a central service table: each provider registers its name, type, address, and quality information; each workflow step queries the table for the exact type it needs. To survive disconnection, the beginner might broadcast the request to neighbors. This breaks in three ways. First, the central table may be unreachable during a network partition. Second, exact matching throws away useful structure: a specialized sensor provider may still be a valid kind of requested sensor provider. Third, broadcast discovery treats every missing answer as a reason to shout louder, increasing messages without giving the system a principled way to prefer a secure, fast, or likely available substitute.
448.ap: The core move is to make the registry both semantic and replicated. Semantic means service types are not just strings; they sit in an ontology, a hierarchy of meanings where one type can be understood as a more specific form of another. Type subsumption is the rule that if a requested general type is needed, a suitable subtype can count as a valid answer. Replicated means the registry is not kept in one fragile place. Eight registry replicas share updates through epidemic gossip, where copies repeatedly exchange what they know so information spreads without a single coordinator. Around this registry, each edge node is modeled as a BDIx agent: it stores beliefs about observed and predicted availability and quality of service, holds desires such as success, latency, and security, and turns the most relevant desires into active intents that drive binding decisions and queries.
448.mech: A workflow begins with concrete steps that need services, such as a sensor provider, an inference engine, and a message broker. Each edge node maintains local beliefs about which services have been observed, how available they seem, and what quality of service they offer. Those beliefs are not treated as perfect truth; they are working estimates in a changing network. The node also has desires, meaning objectives it would like the binding decision to satisfy: finish the workflow, keep latency low, and respect security needs. Deliberation selects which desires matter most now and commits them into intents, the active goals that guide action. When an intent requires a service binding, the node queries SemaReg. The registry compares the requested type with registered service types through the ontology, so it can accept a semantically compatible subtype rather than only an identical label. Registry replicas exchange service knowledge by gossip, so each replica periodically passes updates to others and gradually refreshes the distributed view. In the paper's simulation, 80 heterogeneous BDIx agents and 8 registry replicas run through a three-step IoT workflow under partition conditions. The output is a binding decision for each workflow step, and the evaluation measures whether the full chain succeeds and how much communication the discovery process costs.
448.math: The main mathematical idea is structured matching under uncertainty. Exact matching asks whether two labels are identical. Ontology-based matching asks a richer question: does the available service type sit below, above, or beside the requested type in a meaning hierarchy? Type subsumption is a set relation in plain language: every instance of the narrower type also counts as an instance of the broader type. That makes replacement defensible instead of arbitrary. A second idea is information spreading on a network. Gossip replication works like repeated local averaging of news: each replica shares what it knows with selected peers, and many small exchanges make the whole system less dependent on one path. The tradeoff is freshness versus communication cost; more sharing reduces stale knowledge but consumes bandwidth. The BDIx model adds decision scoring. Beliefs represent uncertain facts about availability and quality, desires define competing goals, and deliberation chooses which goals become active intents. This is not just optimization as a label; it is choosing a binding by balancing what counts as success, delay, and security when the system cannot see the entire network. The abstract supports these concepts, though it does not specify the exact scoring formula.
448.dots: This paper sits near several recurring conference ideas even though its surface vocabulary is edge computing. It is a retrieval problem because a workflow must choose a useful service from a distributed collection. It is a similarity problem because two service descriptions may be different labels for compatible capabilities, and the system must decide which differences matter. It is a graph and network problem because services, agents, and registry replicas are connected by unreliable links, and evidence about availability must travel through those links. It also touches systems tradeoffs: success versus latency, security versus flexibility, and communication overhead versus registry freshness. Compared with recommendation or search papers in the same batch that measure closeness between users, items, or documents, SemaReg measures closeness between service types and uses that closeness to keep a physical workflow alive when the preferred component disappears.
448.ww: The mechanism should beat the naive approach because it removes two brittle assumptions at once. First, it stops assuming that the requested name is the only acceptable answer. If the ontology says an available subtype satisfies the requested functional requirement, the workflow gains a valid fallback without hand-writing every possible substitute. Second, it stops assuming that a single reachable registry has the whole truth. Gossip-based replication gives each region of the edge network a partial but useful copy of service knowledge, so a partition does not automatically erase discovery. The BDIx agent layer helps because binding is not reduced to mere existence. A service that is semantically compatible may still be poor if it is predicted to be unavailable, slow, or insecure. By representing beliefs and goals separately, the node can query and bind in a way that reflects current conditions. This explains why the simulation can show higher workflow success than broadcast discovery while still bounding communication overhead.
448.po: The payoff is a more resilient service discovery layer for disrupted edge IoT workflows. In the reported discrete-event simulation, the system uses 80 heterogeneous agents, including sensor providers, inference engines, and message brokers, with 8 gossip-synchronized registry replicas. For a three-step workflow, SemaReg reaches 90% workflow success at moderate partition levels and improves success by 43% over broadcast discovery. The practical capability is not just finding more services; it is finding acceptable substitutes while limiting the communication cost that would otherwise grow when every failure turns into wider broadcast.
448.limits: The claims rest on the ontology being correct enough that subtype matches really preserve the needed function. If the hierarchy says two services are compatible but their nonfunctional behavior differs in an important way, semantic matching can produce a bad binding. The registry replicas also depend on gossip being frequent and connected enough to keep useful information from becoming stale. The evidence is simulation-based: 80 agents, 8 replicas, and a three-step workflow. The abstract does not prove performance for larger deployments, richer workflows, malicious nodes, wrong quality predictions, or real edge hardware. It also does not specify the full deliberation formula behind the BDIx decisions.

449.bp: The ordinary problem behind this survey is simple: someone has a large image model that already learned broad visual patterns from massive image collections, and now they want to use it for a narrower image classification task. A hospital may need a scanner model, a retailer may need product categories, or a platform may need content labels. Rebuilding the whole model for every new task is expensive because the model contains many adjustable numbers, and full fine-tuning changes all of them. The paper asks how vision transformer models can be adapted without paying that full cost each time. Its object is not a new classifier but the design space of parameter-efficient fine-tuning for vision transformers: ways to keep most of the pretrained visual knowledge intact while changing only a small, carefully chosen part. The survey matters because practical deployment depends on the tradeoff among accuracy, memory, computation, and how easily the approach scales across many downstream tasks.
449.wh: The hard part is that a pretrained vision transformer is both useful and heavy. It is useful because large-scale pretraining has already taught it visual patterns that transfer to image classification tasks. It is heavy because full fine-tuning treats adaptation as if every internal setting might need to move, which raises computation and memory costs. A second difficulty is comparison. Parameter-efficient methods are not one trick with one cost. Additive methods attach small trainable pieces; reparameterization methods describe changes in a compact form; selective methods choose only some parts to update; hybrid methods combine choices; inference-efficient methods care about the cost when the model is used after training. These families trade accuracy, efficiency, and scalability differently. A method that saves training memory may add prediction-time overhead, while a method that is fast at prediction may be less flexible during adaptation. The survey is hard because it must organize this many-sided tradeoff, not merely rank techniques by one score.
449.naive: A smart beginner would take the pretrained vision transformer, copy it for the new image task, and train every adjustable number until the new labels are predicted well. That is full fine-tuning. It is attractive because it gives the model maximum freedom: any part of the visual pipeline can change if the new task needs it. The failure is cost and practicality. If every downstream task needs a separate fully changed copy, memory use grows quickly, training needs large hardware, and deployment becomes harder across many settings. The opposite naive shortcut is to freeze the model and only train a tiny final classifier. That saves cost, but it may not give the model enough room to adapt when the new images require different visual cues.
449.ap: The core idea of the survey is to treat efficient adaptation as a set of design choices about where change is allowed. Instead of asking whether to fine-tune or not, it asks which small part of the model should carry the task-specific information. In additive approaches, the base vision transformer is mostly preserved and small trainable components are inserted or attached. In reparameterization approaches, the change to the model is expressed through a smaller set of numbers rather than a full direct update. In selective approaches, only chosen layers or parameters are opened for training. Hybrid approaches mix these strategies when one kind of restriction is too narrow. Inference-efficient methods add another lens: they ask not only how cheap training is, but how costly the adapted model is when it classifies images later. The paper's central move is a taxonomy that turns a scattered method landscape into comparable mechanical families.
449.mech: The mechanism described by the survey runs as an organizing pipeline rather than as one experimental algorithm. The input is a collection of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods for vision transformers used in image classification. Each method starts from the same broad situation: a pretrained visual model has many internal settings, and a downstream task supplies labeled images that require adaptation. The survey then asks a concrete question of each method: where does the new task information enter the model, and what cost does that choice create? If the method is additive, the changed information sits in extra trainable pieces while the original model mostly stays fixed. If it is reparameterization-based, the method does not store a full free-form change; it stores a compact recipe that produces the needed adjustment. If it is selective, the method chooses a subset of the existing model to update and keeps the rest unchanged. If it is hybrid, it combines two or more of these routes. If it is inference-efficient, it is judged partly by what happens when the model is actually used for prediction. After sorting methods this way, the survey compares their design principles, strengths, limitations, evaluation protocols, and reported results. The output is not a single trained model but a map: for each family, what is saved, what flexibility is lost, and which accuracy-efficiency-scalability tradeoff the method is trying to occupy.
449.math: The main mathematical idea is constrained learning: instead of letting every adjustable number in the model move, the method restricts the search to a smaller set of changes. Learning from examples means defining what counts as a wrong image classification and adjusting allowed settings to reduce that wrongness. Full fine-tuning gives the search many degrees of freedom, which can fit the new task but costs memory and computation. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning deliberately shrinks the set of allowed moves. Additive methods create a small side path whose settings can change while the main path remains stable. Reparameterization methods say that a large possible change can be described through a smaller recipe, so the system searches over the recipe rather than every individual setting. Selective methods choose a few existing locations where movement is most likely to matter. Hybrid methods combine restrictions when one restriction alone gives too little room. The underlying tradeoff is compression versus flexibility: a smaller trainable part is cheaper and easier to store, but it may not express every change the task needs. The survey also uses comparison as a mathematical act: methods are judged by several quantities at once, including accuracy, memory, computation, prediction cost, and scalability. No single number can capture all of these, so the taxonomy is a way to make the tradeoffs visible.
449.dots: This paper sits in the conference's broader efficiency and scalability family. It shares a pressure with edge video adaptation, sparse recommendation representations, distributed parameter-efficient tuning, and privacy-friendly transformer adaptation: large pretrained models are useful, but moving or changing all of their internal state is too expensive for repeated deployment. It also connects to optimization, because every adaptation method must decide what kind of error to reduce and which knobs are allowed to move. It connects to learning from examples, because the hope is that pretrained visual knowledge can be reused rather than relearned. It connects more lightly to systems work, because memory, computation, and prediction-time cost are not secondary details; they decide whether an approach can run in many real settings. The survey's theme, parameter-efficient vision transformers, is therefore a specific version of a recurring 2026 problem: how to reuse a large general model while paying only for the small part that a new task actually needs.
449.ww: The approach works as a survey because the methods it organizes all exploit the same structure in the world: many image tasks share visual building blocks. A model pretrained on massive image data has already learned useful ways to separate edges, textures, parts, shapes, and object-level patterns, even if the abstract does not enumerate those exact features. For a new classification task, the whole visual understanding system often does not need to be rewritten. It needs steering. Parameter-efficient methods work when the new task can be handled by small adjustments to how existing visual evidence is routed, combined, or read out. Additive pieces can carry task-specific corrections while leaving the original model stable. Compact update recipes can capture common directions of change without storing a full new model. Selective training works if the chosen parts are where task-specific decisions concentrate. The taxonomy helps because it explains why different methods succeed for different reasons. It prevents a false comparison where all efficient fine-tuning is treated as the same. Instead, it asks which resource is being saved, where adaptability is preserved, and where the method may have paid for efficiency by giving up expressive room.
449.po: The payoff is a clearer decision map for deploying vision transformers on image classification tasks. The survey gathers parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches into additive-based, reparameterization-based, selective, hybrid, and inference-efficient categories, then analyzes their design principles, strengths, limitations, evaluation protocols, reported results, and tradeoffs. That buys researchers and practitioners a way to reason about method choice without treating efficiency as one vague promise. The practical capability is cheaper adaptation of pretrained vision models across diverse downstream tasks while preserving much of the benefit of large-scale pretraining. The paper also identifies open challenges and future directions for making these methods more reliable, efficient, and deployable.
449.limits: The abstract describes a survey, so its claims are organizational and analytical rather than a new empirical guarantee for one method. The usefulness of the taxonomy depends on whether the reviewed methods are compared under evaluation protocols that are fair enough to reveal real tradeoffs. Parameter-efficient tuning assumes the pretrained vision transformer already contains reusable visual knowledge for the downstream task; if the new task is too different, changing only a small subset of parameters may be insufficient. Efficiency also has several meanings. Saving training memory does not automatically save prediction-time cost, and preserving accuracy on common image classification evaluations does not prove reliability across all deployment settings. The abstract names open challenges but does not prove that they are solved.
